newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS-Brazil government celebrates CVRD victory.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Brazil government celebrates CVRD victory.

text.p: President Fernando Henrique Cardoso celebrated Wednesday his biggest victory in the government's drive to reduce its influence over the Brazilian economy, after successfully selling a controlling stake in mining giant CVRD.
Valepar, an international consortium led by Brazil's largest steelmaker CSN, paid $3.15 billion for 41.73 percent of CVRD's voting stock in an auction on the Rio de Janeiro stock exchange Tuesday.
The auction, to be followed by a share offer to CVRD employees and a global public offer, kicked off the biggest privatization in Latin America.
It is expected to net the government at least $5 billion, with roughly two-thirds of that coming from financing abroad.
The $2 billion expected to flow into Brazil this month to help finance the purchase of the CVRD stake will pad foreign reserves and alleviate some current acount worries, analysts said.
Planning Minister Antonio Kandir said half of the receipts from Tuesday's auction would go toward paying off debt, while the other half would be spent on infrastructure projects across Brazil.
Brazilian reserves fell by about $2 billion last month to around $56 billion, with most of the money paying off interest and amortization on foreign debt.

Analysts hailed the auction as a milestone for economic reform in Brazil, saying Latin America's biggest country was sending the world an important message by showing its commitment to economic liberalization and modernization.
At a briefing this evening in Brasilia, presidential spokesman Sergio Amaral told reporters the president was "happy" with the privatization, which brought in receipts above government expectations.
He also asked Planning Minister Kandir to draw up a list of projets to be financed with cash raised by the CVRD sale, and said the government will press on with its privatization program.
However, legal headaches which have dogged the privatization from the start are expected to plague the new controling shareholders of CVRD for years to come.

A flood of lawsuits and court injunctions against the sell-off managed to delay the auction for a week from its original date of April 29 and continued to pour in even as the hammer went down on the CVRD deal.
Legal experts said it could take anywhere from two to 10 years to hear all the challenges to the CVRD sale, but they did not believe the lawsuits could reverse the outcome of the auction.
CSN Chairman Benjamin Steinbruch, dubbed by Wednesday's newspapers as Brazil's new "King of Steel", said he was confident any legal obstacles would be overcome.
Analysts said Valepar, which was funded by NationsBank Corp, Citibank, George Soros and local pension funds, would directly or indirectly control up to 80 percent of Brazilian steel production.
Besides managing the world's largest iron ore mine, CVRD has a stake in all the major Brazilian steelmakers including CSN.
Steinbruch rejected speculation he might be planning to build a vast steel and iron ore holding, saying CVRD and CSN would continue to operate independently.
He also said the new management would not carry out any "abrupt" changes in CVRD and had no plans to split up the firm.

Steinbruch said he was "comfortable" with the price paid for CVRD, which was too high for rival consortium Valecom composed of Brazil's Votorantim group, South Africa's Anglo-American Corp and a group of Japanese investors.
The stock market, however, was disappointed with the auction price as traders expected a premium higher than the 20 percent Valepar paid over the base price of $25 per share.
CVRD preferred shares plunged 8.09 percent on the Sao Paulo stock exchange Wednesday, the worst performance among blue chips.
((-- Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 507 4151))
